Family Health

Extra nipples and accessory breast tissue

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Some people are born with one or more extra nipples. They may be so small that they are mistaken for a mole or only noticed years later. Most isolated extra nipples do not need treatment. A clinician can confirm what the area is and help if it becomes uncomfortable or changes.

An extra nipple is not always an extra breast

Polythelia refers to additional nipples, while polymastia refers to additional breast tissue. The terms are sometimes used loosely, but the distinction matters: an extra nipple does not necessarily have milk-producing tissue underneath it.

There may be a small nipple alone, a darker area around it or associated glandular tissue. Accessory breast tissue can also occur without a visible nipple, often near an armpit. A detailed classification is less useful for everyday care than knowing which tissue is actually present.

A traditional classification describes the combinations more precisely: type 1 has nipple, areola and glandular tissue; type 2 has nipple and gland but no areola; type 3 has areola and gland but no nipple; and type 4 is glandular tissue alone. Type 5 has nipple and areola over fatty rather than glandular tissue, sometimes called pseudomamma. Type 6 is a nipple alone. These labels describe anatomy, not a sequence of disease severity.

Why it develops

Early in development, breast-related tissue forms along lines running from the armpit towards the groin. Most of that tissue normally disappears apart from the usual breast areas. Tissue that remains elsewhere can form an additional nipple or breast tissue.

This is present from birth even if it is recognised later. Most cases are an isolated variation, although extra nipples can sometimes occur in families or alongside other developmental features. They are not caused by poor hygiene.

The mammary ridges arise from thickened embryonic outer-layer tissue early in pregnancy, beginning around the fourth week. Extra tissue can remain when the portions outside the usual breast sites fail to regress. More than one extra nipple can occur, on one or both sides. Rare ectopic examples are outside the usual milk lines; location alone cannot confirm the diagnosis.

How it can look

An extra nipple may be a small pink or brown mark with a raised centre or tiny dimple. It often lies below a usual nipple but can appear elsewhere.

Appearance alone is not a dependable home test. Moles and other skin growths are not always flat, and a bump along the expected line is not automatically a nipple. Ask a clinician about an unfamiliar lesion, particularly if it is new or changing.

When an extra nipple is found on a baby, mention it at a routine examination so it can be documented. Tell the clinician about any other symptoms or known developmental differences as well.

Changes during puberty, pregnancy or breastfeeding

If glandular tissue is present, it can respond to hormones. The area may become fuller or tender during puberty, around periods or during pregnancy. Functioning accessory tissue can sometimes produce milk after birth.

A tiny extra nipple without glandular tissue will not necessarily behave this way or develop into another breast. New armpit swelling also has other possible causes, so do not assume every lump during pregnancy or breastfeeding is accessory breast tissue.

Ask your maternity team, lactation professional or breast clinic about uncomfortable swelling or leakage. The advice depends on the anatomy and symptoms. Seek prompt assessment for a hot, painful swelling, fever or feeling unwell, because inflammation or infection may need treatment.

Does it mean there is a kidney problem or cancer?

An isolated extra nipple usually does not indicate another disease. Reports of links with urinary-tract abnormalities are inconsistent. An extra nipple alone cannot diagnose kidney disease or predict kidney cancer. A clinician decides whether further assessment is appropriate from the overall examination, history and any other findings.

Accessory breast tissue can develop some of the same benign or malignant conditions as usual breast tissue. This is a reason to check a new change, not a reason to regard every extra nipple as a cancer warning.

Do not rely on a claim that one named gene makes an extra nipple cancerous. Research on mammary development does not provide that kind of individual prediction.

Changes that should be checked

Book a clinical review for a new lump, persistent thickening, an unexplained change in size, a non-healing sore or rash, or unusual discharge. Blood-stained discharge and a firm new lump should not be dismissed because the area has always been called an extra nipple.

Tell the clinician about accessory tissue when discussing breast symptoms or screening. Follow the screening plan appropriate to your age and risk, and ask whether the extra tissue needs any specific assessment. Routine checks cannot guarantee prevention of every possible problem.

Removal is optional for many people

If the area is comfortable and the diagnosis is clear, leaving it alone is often appropriate. Removal may be considered for persistent discomfort, symptoms or personal preference.

Surgery is not a non-invasive procedure. Its extent depends on whether there is just a small nipple or deeper glandular tissue. Ask about scarring, sensation, bleeding, infection, anaesthesia and recovery before deciding. A simple removal and a larger accessory-tissue operation are not the same procedure.

For a child, discuss timing and the child’s preferences as they grow. There is usually no need to treat an otherwise harmless extra nipple as an urgent cosmetic problem.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

DermNet distinguishes extra nipples from accessory glandular tissue and describes the anatomical classification and hormonal response.

Most isolated findings need no treatment; persistent lumps, unusual discharge or skin changes merit assessment, and kidney associations are not a diagnostic rule.

How BeMama can help

Ask which tissue is present, what changes to watch for and whether symptoms or personal preferences justify removal.

When to seek help

A new firm lump, blood-stained discharge, persistent rash or hot painful swelling with fever needs clinical assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Most isolated extra nipples are harmless and need no treatment.
  • An extra nipple and extra glandular breast tissue are not the same thing.
  • Hormonal swelling or milk production depends on the tissue present.
  • New lumps, unusual discharge or persistent skin changes deserve assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Can an extra nipple look like a mole?

Yes. A small extra nipple can be difficult to distinguish from another skin mark. A clinician can assess an uncertain or changing area.

Will every extra nipple produce milk?

No. Milk production requires functioning glandular tissue, which is not present under every extra nipple.

Do I need it removed to prevent cancer?

Removal is not routinely required for a harmless isolated extra nipple. Any suspicious change needs assessment, and a clinician can explain the appropriate options.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
